etymology: From the Old English dros, “dregs, scum,” the worthless refuse cast off from metal in the fire of the refiner.
biblical_def: Dross is the impure refuse that rises to the surface and is skimmed away when silver or gold is melted in the furnace; it is the worthless residue that the fire separates from the precious metal. In Scripture it is a standing figure for the wicked and for sin, which must be purged from God’s people as dross is purged from silver. The Psalmist confesses, “Thou puttest away all the wicked of the earth like dross” (Psa 119:119), and Solomon teaches, “Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer” (Pro 25:4). Isaiah laments backslidden Jerusalem: “thy silver is become dross” (Isa 1:22), and then promises the refining mercy of God: “I will turn my hand upon thee, and purely purge away thy dross” (Isa 1:25). By Ezekiel the LORD declares that the house of Israel is become dross, and He will gather them into the furnace to melt them (Eze 22:18–19). The image teaches the holiness of God and the necessity of sanctification: the believer is the silver, his corruptions the dross, and his afflictions the refiner’s fire. God does not cast the silver away with the dross; He purges the dross that the silver may shine. So the fiery trial is no accident but the loving labour of the Refiner, who sits over the furnace until His own image is seen in the metal.
webster_summary: The worthless refuse skimmed from metal in the furnace; in Scripture a figure of the wicked and of sin to be purged away.
webster_full: DROSS, the scum or refuse cast off from metals in melting.
It is the worthless residue the fire separates from precious silver.
In Scripture it figures the wicked, whom God puts away (Psa 119:119).
It figures sin, which the refiner’s fire purges from the saints (Isa 1:25).
Backslidden Israel is called dross, gathered into the furnace (Eze 22:18).
scriptures: Thou puttest away all the wicked of the earth like dross: therefore I love thy testimonies.
Pro 25:4
Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer.
Isa 1:25
And I will turn my hand upon thee, and purely purge away thy dross, and take away all thy tin:
Son of man, the house of Israel is to me become dross: all they are brass, and tin, and iron, and lead, in the midst of the furnace; they are even the dross of silver.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses the refining of God’s people from the dross of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the holiness of God in the refining of His people. As dross is the worthless refuse that the fire drives out of the silver, so corruption is the dross of the soul, which God purges by the heat of affliction. He does not melt His people to destroy them but to purify them; the furnace is the instrument of sanctification, and the dross that rises is meant to be skimmed away, that the pure metal may be left.

The image also rebukes the man who is content with his dross, mistaking the impure mass for true silver. Isaiah charged Jerusalem that her silver was become dross, her worship and her righteousness debased and adulterated. The Refiner’s mercy is that He will not leave His own in that state: “I will… purely purge away thy dross.” The saint should therefore neither despise the chastening of the LORD nor faint under it, but yield to the fire, knowing the Refiner sits over the furnace until He sees His image in the metal.
roots_summary: The word means the refuse of metal, the impurity the fire drives out of the silver.

The pure silver left behind figures the sanctified believer.
usage: Like dross from silver, the LORD purges the corruptions of His people by the fire of affliction.
Dross teaches that the furnace of trial is the loving labour of the Refiner, not His wrath.
Beware the man content with his dross, mistaking adulterated worship for true silver.

etymology: From pot and the Old English sceard, “a fragment,” a broken piece of earthen vessel.
biblical_def: A potsherd is a broken fragment of a fired clay pot, the most common and worthless of refuse, fit only to be cast on the ash-heap or used to scrape and scoop. Job, smitten with sore boils from head to foot, sat down among the ashes and “took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal” (Job 2:8), the picture of a man brought to the dust of utter affliction. The suffering Messiah of the twenty-second Psalm cries, “My strength is dried up like a potsherd” (Psa 22:15), parched and broken in the agony of the cross. Isaiah sets the potsherd against its Maker to rebuke the pride of the creature: “Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth” (Isa 45:9) — as if a shard of clay should contend with the Potter who formed it. Solomon likens flattering lips over a wicked heart to “a potsherd covered with silver dross” (Pro 26:23), a worthless thing glazed to look precious. The potsherd thus teaches the frailty and lowliness of man, who is but clay, easily broken and quickly cast aside; and it magnifies the sovereignty of the Potter, who has power over the clay to make one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour. The shard cannot answer back; it can only be shaped or shattered at the will of Him who made it.
webster_summary: A broken fragment of an earthen pot; in Scripture a figure of man’s frailty and lowliness before his Maker.
webster_full: POTSHERD, a broken piece or fragment of an earthen vessel.
Job took a potsherd to scrape himself in his affliction (Job 2:8).
The suffering Messiah’s strength is dried like a potsherd (Psa 22:15).
The potsherd may not strive with the Potter who formed it (Isa 45:9).
Flattery over a wicked heart is a potsherd glazed with silver dross (Pro 26:23).
scriptures: Job 2:8
And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes.
My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death.
Isa 45:9
Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?
Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses the frailty of man and the sovereignty of the Potter.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the sovereignty of the Potter over the clay. A potsherd is but a broken shard of fired earth, and Isaiah’s woe falls upon the creature who would strive with the Maker that formed him: shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? Man, who is dust, has no standing to contend with God over His decrees; the shard cannot answer the hand that shaped it. To know oneself a potsherd is the beginning of humility before the throne.

The potsherd also preaches the frailty of our estate and the depth of Christ’s sufferings. Job sat in the ashes and scraped his sores with a shard; the Saviour cried that His strength was dried up like a potsherd as He was brought into the dust of death. Our days are brittle as fired clay, soon broken and cast aside; and the Lord of glory was content to be made low as a potsherd, that He might lift His people from the ash-heap and make of broken clay a vessel unto honour.
roots_summary: The word joins pot and sherd, a fragment, naming a broken piece of earthen vessel.

The potsherd may not strive with the Potter who made it.
It figures the frailty and lowliness of man before God.
usage: Like a potsherd, man is but brittle clay, easily broken and quickly cast aside.
The potsherd that may not strive with its Maker rebukes all pride against God’s sovereign decrees.
Christ’s strength dried like a potsherd shows how low the Saviour stooped to raise His people.

etymology: From earthen, made of clay or baked earth, and vessel, a container; a pot of fired clay, common and fragile.
biblical_def: An earthen vessel is a container formed of clay and hardened in the fire, the commonest and cheapest of household ware, prized not for its worth but for what it holds. Scripture turns this lowly object into one of its richest figures of the gospel. Paul writes, “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7). The treasure is the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ; the earthen vessels are the weak, mortal, breakable ministers and saints who carry it. God lodges His infinite riches in fragile clay on purpose, that the surpassing power may be plainly seen to be His and not the vessel’s. Jeremiah was bidden to put the deeds of purchase “in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days” (Jer 32:14), a token that the covenant promise would outlast the exile. Lamentations mourns that the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, are esteemed “as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter” (Lam 4:2). The earthen vessel thus teaches that God delights to use weak and despised instruments, that no flesh should glory in His presence. The vessel is common; the treasure is glorious; and the contrast is the very point, that the power may be of God.
webster_summary: A common pot of fired clay; in Scripture a figure of the weak saints who carry the treasure of the gospel.
webster_full: EARTHEN VESSEL, a container made of clay and baked in the fire.
It is the commonest and cheapest of household ware.
The gospel treasure is borne in earthen vessels (2Co 4:7).
The excellency of the power is thereby seen to be of God, not man.
Jeremiah’s deeds of purchase were kept in an earthen vessel (Jer 32:14).

Lam 4:2

Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days.
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that God lodges His treasure in weak clay that the power may be His.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is that the excellency of the power is of God and not of us. He puts the treasure of the gospel into earthen vessels on purpose — into weak, mortal, breakable ministers and saints — so that the surpassing glory of the work may plainly be seen to be His. The vessel is common clay; the treasure within is the light of the knowledge of the glory of God. The very meanness of the container magnifies the riches of what it holds.

This rebukes both the pride that would glory in the vessel and the despair that would despise it. No flesh may boast, for the worth is in the treasure, not the pot; yet no saint need faint at his own weakness, for God chose the clay that the power might be His. The minister cracked and pressed on every side still carries the unsearchable riches of Christ; and the breaking of the vessel only lets the light shine the more. So we are troubled, yet not distressed, that the life of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh.
roots_summary: The phrase joins earthen, of baked clay, and vessel, a container, naming a common clay pot.

The weakness of the vessel magnifies the power of God.

etymology: From the Old English belg, “bag,” an instrument that draws in and drives out air to blow the refiner’s fire to a fiercer heat.
biblical_def: The bellows is the refiner’s instrument, a bag or chamber worked by hand or foot to force a blast of air into the furnace, raising the fire to the heat needed to melt metal and separate it from its dross. It appears in Scripture in a single solemn place, where the LORD by Jeremiah declares the failure of His refining judgment upon a people who would not be purified: “The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away” (Jer 6:29). The picture is of a refining furnace driven so long and so hot that the very bellows are scorched and the lead flux burned up, yet the metal yields no pure silver, only “reprobate silver” (Jer 6:30), for the dross will not part from it. So the prophet pronounces a people refined in vain, judgment poured out and chastisement multiplied, and still no repentance comes forth. The bellows thus stands as a sobering witness that the fire of affliction, which softens and purifies the elect, only hardens the reprobate, who are refined and yet not purged. The same furnace that brings forth a vessel for the finer leaves the obstinate as rejected silver. God’s refining is never wasted upon His own; but where the heart is finally set against Him, even the fiercest blast of the bellows melts in vain.
webster_summary: The refiner’s instrument for blowing the fire hotter; in Jeremiah a figure of judgment that refines the reprobate in vain.
webster_full: BELLOWS, an instrument that drives air to blow a fire hotter.
It raises the refiner’s furnace to the heat that melts metal.
In Jeremiah the bellows are burned and the founder melts in vain (Jer 6:29).
The wicked are not plucked away though refined in the fire.
It figures judgment that hardens, not purges, the reprobate heart.
scriptures: Jer 6:29
The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away.
Jer 6:30
Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the LORD hath rejected them.
Jer 6:28
They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters.

As they gather silver, and brass, and iron, and lead, and tin, into the midst of the furnace, to blow the fire upon it, to melt it; so will I gather you in mine anger and in my fury, and I will leave you there, and melt you.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the fire which purges the elect hardens the reprobate in vain.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the solemn truth that the same fire which refines the elect only hardens the reprobate. The bellows blow the furnace to its fiercest heat, the lead flux is consumed, the founder labours on; yet the wicked are not plucked away, and the metal comes forth as reprobate silver. Judgment and affliction are not in themselves saving; they soften the vessel God is purifying and harden the vessel He has rejected. The fire reveals what the heart already is.

This rebukes the presumption that mere suffering must do a man good. Israel was refined and refined, the bellows burned with the long labour of God’s chastening, and still no repentance came forth, for the dross would not part from the silver. Where God works grace, the furnace purges; where the heart is finally set against Him, the founder melts in vain. Let no man trust in his trials as if affliction itself could save; only the Refiner’s own hand, working faith and repentance, brings the pure metal forth.
roots_summary: The word comes from belg, a bag, naming the instrument that blows air to feed the refiner’s fire.
roots_lines: Bellows — Old English belg, “bag.”

It raises the refiner’s furnace to a fiercer heat.
In Jeremiah the burned bellows figure refining in vain.
The reprobate silver is rejected though long in the fire.
usage: Like the burned bellows, judgment refines the reprobate in vain when the heart will not yield.
The bellows teach that the same fire which purges the elect hardens the obstinate.
Let no man trust in mere suffering, for affliction without grace melts the founder in vain.

etymology: From plumb, a weight of lead (Latin plumbum), and line, a cord; a lead weight on a string that hangs true to test whether a wall is upright.
biblical_def: A plumbline is the builder’s tool of exact judgment: a cord weighted with lead that, hung beside a wall, falls straight by gravity and reveals whether the wall stands true or leans to its fall. The LORD took it up as the very emblem of His righteous standard in the vision of Amos: “Behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand… Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more” (Amo 7:7–8). The wall of Israel, once built upright, had bowed away from the rule of God’s law, and the plumbline exposed the lean that doomed it. So in the judgment of Jerusalem the LORD says, “I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab” (2Ki 21:13), measuring her by the same true standard that condemned the north. Isaiah promises that in Zion God will “lay judgment to the line, and righteousness to the plummet” (Isa 28:17). The plumbline teaches that God judges not by shifting human opinion but by a fixed and perfect standard, His own holy law, against which every life, every nation, and every church is measured. A wall may look upright to the careless eye, yet the plumbline shows the truth; and what leans from the rule of God, however fair it seems, is marked for ruin.
webster_summary: A lead weight on a cord that tests whether a wall stands upright; in Amos God’s emblem of His fixed standard of judgment.
webster_full: PLUMBLINE, a cord weighted with lead that hangs true by gravity.

He measured Jerusalem by line and plummet in judgment (2Ki 21:13).
He lays judgment to the line and righteousness to the plummet (Isa 28:17).

Thus he shewed me: and, behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand.
Amo 7:8

And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.
Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses God’s fixed and righteous standard of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is that God judges by a fixed and perfect standard, not by the shifting opinions of men. The plumbline hangs true by an unchanging law of weight; just so the LORD measures His people by the unchanging rule of His holy law. A wall may look upright to the careless eye, but the plumbline shows the lean that dooms it. So lives, nations, and churches that seem fair are tried against God’s righteousness, and what bends from His rule is marked for ruin.

The plumbline rebukes every attempt to make man the measure of right and wrong. The wall does not judge the plumbline; the plumbline judges the wall. God will not bend His standard to the crookedness of the age, nor pass by the lean He has exposed: “I will not again pass by them any more.” The only safety is to be built true to the rule, and where a man has bowed away from it, to be set upright again by repentance, conformed afresh to the perfect law that is the line and the plummet of the LORD.
roots_summary: The word joins plumb, a lead weight, and line, a cord, naming the tool that tests a wall’s uprightness.
roots_lines: Plumb — Latin plumbum, “lead.”
Line — a cord on which the weight hangs.

usage: Like a plumbline, God’s law tries every life and nation by a fixed and perfect standard.
The plumbline teaches that the wall does not judge the rule, but the rule judges the wall.
What leans from the line of God’s law, however fair it seems, is marked for ruin.

etymology: From measure and line; a cord or surveyor’s line stretched out to mark off and measure land or a building.
biblical_def: A measuring line is the surveyor’s cord, stretched out to mark off bounds, measure a wall, or lay out a city, an instrument of ordered apportionment and exact design. In Zechariah the prophet sees “a man with a measuring line in his hand” going forth to measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof and the length thereof (Zec 2:1–2), a vision of the city’s restoration, so peopled and blessed that it shall be inhabited as towns without walls. Jeremiah promises that the rebuilt city shall extend by the measuring line: “the measuring line shall yet go forth over against it upon the hill Gareb” (Jer 31:39), every cubit consecrated holy unto the LORD. In Ezekiel’s vision of the temple a man stands with “a line of flax in his hand, and a measuring reed” to lay out the house of God with exactness (Eze 40:3). And the LORD Himself challenges Job, asking who laid the measures of the earth and “who hath stretched the line upon it” (Job 38:5), for the Maker measured out creation with perfect design. The measuring line thus teaches the deliberate, ordered, and gracious purpose of God, who measures out the bounds of His people’s habitation, lays the dimensions of His house, and apportions to His own a goodly heritage. The line that surveys for judgment in some places here surveys for blessing, marking off what God will build and bless.
webster_summary: A surveyor’s cord for measuring land or building; in the prophets a figure of God’s ordered purpose to build and bless.
webster_full: MEASURING LINE, a cord stretched out to measure land or a building.
It marks off bounds and lays out a city with order.
A man measures Jerusalem with a measuring line (Zec 2:1–2).
The line lays out the dimensions of God’s temple (Eze 40:3).
God stretched the line upon the earth at creation (Job 38:5).

I lifted up mine eyes again, and looked, and behold a man with a measuring line in his hand.
Zec 2:2
Then said I, Whither goest thou? And he said unto me, To measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof, and what is the length thereof.
And the measuring line shall yet go forth over against it upon the hill Gareb, and shall compass about to Goath.
Job 38:5
Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line upon it?
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses the ordered and gracious purpose of God to build and bless His people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the deliberate and ordered purpose of God, who does nothing by chance but measures all by design. The man with the measuring line goes forth to lay out Jerusalem; the line of flax surveys the temple; the LORD Himself stretched the line upon the earth at its founding. God is not a God of confusion but of order, and He measures out the bounds of His people’s habitation and the dimensions of His house with a wisdom that misses nothing.

Where the plumbline tries a wall for judgment, the measuring line here often surveys for blessing, marking off what God will build and inhabit. The vision of Zechariah promises a Jerusalem so blessed it overflows its walls; Jeremiah promises a city whose every measured cubit is holy unto the LORD. So the saint may rest in the truth that the lines are fallen unto him in pleasant places, for the same God who measured creation apportions to His own a goodly heritage, and surveys with grace the place He has prepared to build and to bless.

etymology: From the Latin aqua marina, “sea water,” the modern name for the blue-green variety of beryl, the stone the KJV simply calls “beryl.”
biblical_def: The word aquamarine does not appear in the Authorized Version; it is the modern name for the sea-green and blue member of the beryl family, and the KJV knows this whole family of precious stones simply as “beryl.” Beryl is a stone of honour in Scripture. It was set in the high priest’s breastplate as the first stone of the fourth row: “the fourth row a beryl, and an onyx, and a jasper” (Exo 28:20), one of the twelve graven each with the name of a tribe of Israel, that Aaron might bear the names of God’s people upon his heart before the LORD. Beryl shone among the precious stones that covered the anointed cherub in Eden (Eze 28:13). The beloved’s hands in the Song are “as gold rings set with the beryl” (Son 5:14). And in the new Jerusalem beryl is named the eighth foundation of the wall of the city: “the eighth, beryl” (Rev 21:20). So this sea-green stone, which men now call aquamarine, is woven into the worship of God, the glory of His sanctuary, and the splendour of the city to come. It teaches that the LORD adorns His house and His people with what is precious and enduring, and that the names of His own are borne, jewel-like, upon the breastplate and built, jewel-like, into the everlasting walls. What men prize as a costly gem, God takes up as a token of His covenant love.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is that “aquamarine” is simply the modern name for the blue-green beryl the Authorized Version calls “beryl,” and that God takes up such precious stones as tokens of His covenant. Beryl was set in the high priest’s breastplate, graven with the name of a tribe, that the names of God’s people might be borne upon Aaron’s heart before the LORD. What men prize as a costly gem, God appoints to carry the memory of His own into His presence.

The same stone is built into the foundations of the new Jerusalem, the eighth course of the wall of the city of God. So beryl runs from the breastplate of the old covenant to the everlasting city of the new, a thread of sea-green glory from Sinai to the throne. The lesson is that the LORD adorns His house and His people with what is precious and enduring; the saints, like living stones, are gathered into a building more glorious than any earthly gem, and the names borne jewel-like on the breastplate are at last built jewel-like into walls that shall not pass away.

etymology: From the Latin thesaurus, “a store, hoard,” through the Old French tresorie; a place where wealth or sacred offerings are stored.
biblical_def: A treasury is the place where wealth, tribute, or the offerings of God’s house are stored and kept. Under the old covenant the spoil of Jericho, the silver and gold and vessels of brass and iron, was consecrated and brought “into the treasury of the house of the LORD” (Jos 6:19, 24). In the temple of the second covenant stood the treasury where the people cast their offerings, and there our Lord sat and watched: “Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much” (Mar 12:41). Then came a poor widow who threw in two mites, which make a farthing; and the Lord called His disciples and said that she had cast in more than they all, “for all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living” (Mar 12:44; Luk 21:1–4). When the chief priests took the betrayal-money Judas flung down, they said it was not lawful to put it “into the treasury, because it is the price of blood” (Mat 27:6), scrupling over the vessel while plotting murder. The treasury thus becomes a place of searching judgment, where God weighs not the amount but the heart of the giver. The widow’s two mites, weighed in the treasury of heaven, outshine the rich man’s heaped abundance, for the LORD measures the gift by the love and the sacrifice from which it flows.
webster_summary: A place where wealth or sacred offerings are stored; the temple treasury where the widow cast her two mites.
webster_full: TREASURY, a place where wealth or offerings are stored and kept.
The spoil of Jericho was brought into the treasury of the LORD (Jos 6:24).
Jesus sat over against the temple treasury and watched the givers (Mar 12:41).
A poor widow cast in two mites, all her living (Mar 12:44).
The priests would not put the price of blood into the treasury (Mat 27:6).
scriptures: And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much.
For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.
Luk 21:1
And he looked up, and saw the rich men casting their gifts into the treasury.
Mat 27:6
And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; the treasury witnesses that God weighs the heart of the giver, not the amount of the gift.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is that God weighs not the amount of a gift but the heart from which it flows. Christ sat over against the treasury and watched; the rich cast in much of their abundance, but the poor widow cast in two mites of her want, and the Lord judged that she had given more than all the rest, for she gave all her living. In the treasury of heaven the smallest gift offered in faith and love outweighs the largest given out of surplus and self.

The treasury also rebukes a religion that is scrupulous about outward forms while harbouring inward corruption. The chief priests would not defile the treasury with the price of blood, yet they had paid that price to betray innocent blood, straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel. So the treasury searches the giver: it exposes both the widow’s costly love and the hypocrite’s hollow nicety. What a man does with his substance before the eye of God is a true gauge of his heart, for where his treasure is, there will his heart be also.
roots_summary: The word comes from thesaurus, a store or hoard, naming the place where wealth and offerings are kept.

The widow’s two mites outweighed the rich man’s abundance.

The treasury teaches that God weighs the heart of the giver, not the amount of the gift.
What a man does with his substance before God’s eye is a true gauge of his heart.

etymology: From the Middle English welthe, “well-being, riches,” akin to weal; abundance of possessions or worldly goods.
biblical_def: Wealth is abundance of possessions, riches, and worldly substance. Scripture treats it as a thing neither good nor evil in itself but tested entirely by its source and its use. The LORD is its giver: “thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth” (Deu 8:18), so that all increase is His gift and held in trust. A good man may rightly leave an inheritance to his children’s children, and “the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just” (Pro 13:22). Yet Scripture sets a strait limit on the trust a man may put in his riches, for they cannot purchase the one thing needful: “They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches; none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him” (Psa 49:6–7). Therefore Paul charges the rich “that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God… that they be rich in good works… laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come” (1Ti 6:17–19). Wealth, then, is a stewardship and a snare at once: received as God’s gift it may serve much good; clutched as a man’s god it damns the soul. The believer is to hold it with an open hand, knowing he brought nothing into this world and can carry nothing out, and to lay up his true treasure where neither moth nor rust corrupts.
webster_summary: Abundance of worldly possessions; a stewardship from God when received in trust, a snare when made a man’s god.
webster_full: WEALTH, abundance of possessions or worldly substance.
It is God’s gift, for He gives the power to get wealth (Deu 8:18).
It is held in trust and may serve much good in the just.
It cannot redeem the soul nor ransom a brother (Psa 49:6–7).
The rich are charged to trust God, not uncertain riches (1Ti 6:17).
scriptures: Deu 8:18
But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers, as it is this day.
A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
Psa 49:6
They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches;
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel makes wealth the proof and prize of faith; Scripture names the love of mammon a snare and idolatry to be rebuked.
corruption_paragraphs: Against the plain teaching of Scripture stands the prosperity gospel, the false doctrine that godliness is a means of gain, that faith is a lever to pull worldly riches from the hand of God, and that material wealth is the sure mark of His favour. This is the very error Paul names and condemns: men “of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself” (1Ti 6:5). The Lord Himself drew the line that no man may cross: “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). To preach wealth as the prize of faith is to baptize the love of money, which is the root of all evil, and to turn the gospel of a crucified Saviour into a scheme of self-enrichment. It flatters the flesh, robs the poor saint of comfort by implying his poverty is unbelief, and dethrones Christ in favour of gold.

Scripture rebukes this on its own ground. The Lord Jesus, who was rich, for our sakes became poor (2Co 8:9), and warned that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. The true riches are not silver and gold but the unsearchable riches of Christ, and the man whom God blesses with worldly wealth is made a steward, not an owner, charged to be rich in good works and ready to distribute. The love of mammon is idolatry, setting the gift in the place of the Giver; and the heart that hoards its treasure on earth proves itself a stranger to the treasure laid up in heaven. Let the rich hold their wealth with an open hand, and let none measure the favour of God by the fullness of a purse.
roots_summary: The word comes from welthe, well-being or riches, akin to weal, naming abundance of worldly goods.
roots_lines: Wealth — Middle English welthe, “well-being, riches.”

usage: Like all wealth, riches are God’s gift held in trust, to be used in good works, not hoarded.

etymology: From the Old French wage, “pledge, pay,” the hire or recompense due to a labourer for his work.
biblical_def: Wages are the hire and just recompense due to a labourer for his work, and Scripture guards the labourer’s right with a jealous care. The law of God forbids the master to withhold or delay them: “Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning” (Lev 19:13). The Lord Jesus affirms the principle in the gospel, “for the labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luk 10:7), and James pronounces a fearful woe upon those who grind the poor: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth” (Jas 5:4). But Scripture also takes up the word to name the dreadful recompense of sin. As an honest day’s work earns an honest wage, so sin earns its own certain pay: “the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom 6:23). Here is the great contrast of the gospel: death is wages, earned and owed and paid in full to every sinner; but eternal life is a gift, free and undeserved, given in Christ. Wages thus stands at the heart of two truths — the justice that requires the labourer be paid, and the justice that pays the sinner the death his sin has earned, save where free grace intervenes.
webster_summary: The hire due to a labourer for his work; in Scripture also the certain recompense of sin, which is death.
webster_full: WAGES, the hire or recompense due to a labourer for his work.
The law forbids withholding the hired man’s wages overnight (Lev 19:13).
The labourer is worthy of his hire (Luk 10:7).
The withheld hire of the reapers cries to the Lord of sabaoth (Jas 5:4).
The wages of sin is death; eternal life is the gift of God (Rom 6:23).
scriptures: Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning.
Rom 6:23
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Luk 10:7
And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house.
Jas 5:4

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
corruption_summary: The oppression of the labourer robs the poor of his just hire; and the deceit of sin hides the deadly wage every sinner truly earns.
corruption_paragraphs: A double corruption attaches to this word, and Scripture rebukes both. The first is the oppression of the labourer — the withholding, docking, or fraudulent delay of the hire that is justly his. The law of God set its face against it: the hired man’s wages must not so much as remain overnight. James thunders that the kept-back hire of the reapers cries aloud, and that those cries have entered the ears of the Lord of sabaoth, who hears the poor and will avenge them. To defraud a workman of his pay, to enrich oneself on unpaid toil, is no small sin but a crime that calls down the judgment of heaven; the gospel that frees the soul does not loose the master’s duty to pay his servant justly.

The second corruption is subtler: the deceit by which sin hides its true wage. The world offers sin as pleasure and gain, never disclosing the recompense written into its very nature — “the wages of sin is death.” Sin is a labour that earns, exactly and inexorably, the death of body and soul; the sinner is paid in full what his sin has truly merited. The lie of the tempter, from the garden onward, is that the wage will not be paid, that “ye shall not surely die.” Against this stands the gospel’s sharp distinction: death is wages, earned and owed; but eternal life is a gift, free in Christ, who took the wage of sin upon Himself that His people might receive the unearned gift of life.
